title: The services page a B2B SaaS company actually needs
metaTitle: The services page a B2B SaaS company needs
excerpt: Each service on the page needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step. For this buyer the next step is to book a demo, in their words.
alt: A close view of a fountain pen writing on lined paper. The article is about writing each service so a buyer can read the outcome and the limit.
caption: A services block should be specific enough to write by hand. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a services block contain?
faqs.answer: Write the job in the buyer's words, the outcome that will be true when the work is done, and the boundary of what you will not take on. End with how to book a demo and what that call will decide. A block missing any of those is not ready to publish.

faqs.question: Why do capability grids fail on a services page?
faqs.answer: Labels such as strategy or partnership do not say what changes in the buyer's week, and they give no fence. Different sizes of work become twins. Replace the grid with blocks a person can read aloud and retell.

faqs.question: How many services should the page list?
faqs.answer: List the offers you can deliver without inventing a team. For many companies that is a simple start and a heavier version for a messier setup. Leave an unfinished offer off the page until its boundary is real.

markdown:
A B2B SaaS company services page should list the work in the buyer's language. An operator who already has software does not need a grid of capabilities. They need each offer stated as an outcome, a boundary, and a next step. The next step is to book a demo.

If a block cannot say what will be true when the work is done, what you will not take on, and how to start, it is not ready to publish. Vague lines such as "strategic enablement" reassure the team that wrote them. They give the operator nothing to forward to a colleague.

## Write the job, not the department

Buyers do not shop your org chart. They shop a result they can imagine on a Tuesday. "We implement the product in your billing workflow" is a job. "Professional services" is a department. Use the job as the heading. Keep the internal name in a contract if you must. It does not have to lead the page.

Speak the way the operator speaks. Approvals, seats, records, the quarter close, the support inbox. If your team says "workstream" and the buyer says "the weekly report," use the weekly report. Google's people-first content guidance is plain about this kind of page. Useful content answers a real question from experience you actually have, in words the reader would use. A services page stuffed with category language answers a question nobody asked.

One service per block. A block that covers onboarding, custom integration, and training has not decided what it is selling. Split them, or pick the one you want this page to sell and link the others only if they are real offers with their own boundaries.

Name who the service is for in the first line of the block. A finance lead replacing a spreadsheet. An admin rolling the tool out to forty people. A founder who will do the configuration themselves and only wants a review. The same product can support all three. The service should not pretend they are one person.

## The outcome

The outcome is a change in the operator's week, not a list of activities. "Your team approves invoices in the product instead of in email" is an outcome. "We run workshops" is an activity. Activities can support the outcome. They should not replace it.

Write the outcome so a skeptical colleague can test it. What will exist that does not exist now? A live workspace. A migrated file. A role map. An admin who can add a seat without you. If you cannot point at the artifact, the outcome is still a mood.

Keep the outcome inside what the software and your team can actually do. Promising a faster close when you only configure a dashboard is how demos turn into refunds. Stay with the change you will stand behind. A smaller true outcome beats a larger hoped one.

Add the condition when the outcome depends on them. "Once we have a sample of last month's records." "Once a single owner is named on your side." Conditions are part of the outcome. Hidden conditions are how projects sour.

Two or three sentences are enough. A services block that needs a scroll to reach the point has started to perform thoroughness. Thoroughness belongs in the statement of work, after they have booked.

## The boundary

Every service needs a fence. The fence is what makes the outcome believable. Without it, the operator hears an unlimited promise and either distrusts you or arrives with a scope you did not price.

State the boundary in the same block as the outcome. Number of workflows. Number of systems you will connect. What "done" means. What remains their job. Data cleaning. Internal politics. The email to their own team. You can be polite and still be specific.

A useful boundary sounds like this. "We configure the approval chain for one entity and train two admins. We do not rebuild your chart of accounts." The operator can feel the size. They can also see whether they need a different offer.

If you have a menu, show the menu. A fixed onboarding. A heavier migration. A monthly office hour. Each with its own fence. A single blob called "success" forces every buyer into a custom argument. Custom can exist for the odd case. It should not be the only shape on the page.

The boundary also protects your product story. If the homepage shows the product in use, the services page should not imply that the product does nothing until a long project finishes. Say what works on the day they get access, and what the service adds. Operators who already run software are alert to tools that only function after a retainer.

## The next step is a demo

Each block ends by telling them how to book a demo, and what the demo will decide. The call is not a generic hello. It is where you confirm that their outcome fits your boundary.

Say what happens on the call. You look at their current step. You say whether the fixed onboarding fits. You say if they need the heavier block, or if they need no services at all. An operator trusts a page that is willing to send them away from paid help.

Tell them what to bring. A sketch of the workflow. The name of the system beside yours. The person who will own it after you leave. Three items, not a dossier. A long prep list is a way to postpone the click.

One action per block, and it should be the same kind of action. "Book a demo." If a light offer can start by email, you may say so, but do not invent a second maze. The page's job is to get the right people into a conversation with the fence already visible. Label the button with the demo, not with "learn more." Learn more is the page they are already on.

Put the action at the end of the block, and once in the introduction for the person who already knows which offer they want. Repeating it under every heading is fine when each heading is a different offer. Repeating three different verbs is not.

## Why a capability grid fails

A grid of six icons feels like a services page because it is shaped like one. The labels give it away. Strategy. Innovation. Partnership. Excellence. None of those is an outcome. None has a fence. The next step, if there is one, sits in the corner of the page as a form that asks what they are interested in. They do not know. You refused to say.

The grid also flattens different sizes of work. A two-hour admin review and a six-week migration become twins. The operator cannot tell which one they are buying, so they either ask for everything or ask for nothing.

Replace the grid with blocks you can read aloud. If a block cannot survive being read to a buyer without extra explanation, it is not finished. Cut it or rewrite it. An empty slot on the page is better than a tile that creates a bad call.

Keep a short index at the top if you have more than three offers. The index is a table of contents, in their words, linking to the blocks. It is not a second grid of abstractions.

## How many offers to publish

Publish the offers you can deliver without inventing a team you do not have. For many companies that is two. A start, and a heavier version for a messier setup. A third, advisory and occasional, if you truly run it.

Four or more can be honest when the product is sold into genuinely different jobs. A billing rollout and a support-desk rollout are different services even if the software is one codebase. Give them separate outcomes and separate fences. Do not merge them to make the page look simpler than the work.

If you are still designing an offer, leave it off. A coming-soon tile collects the wrong demos. You can add the block the week the boundary is real.

Order the blocks by the path most operators should take, not by the price you prefer. The recommended start comes first. The heavy migration comes after, for the reader who recognized themselves in the boundary. A small note can say "most teams begin here." That is guidance, not a trick.

## A block you can ship

Use this shape and fill it with your real work.

1. Heading in the buyer's words. The job, not the department.
2. Who it is for, in one sentence.
3. The outcome. What will be true, and on what condition.
4. The boundary. What you will do, and what you will not.
5. What they keep when you are done. Access, an admin, a written map.
6. Book a demo. What the call decides, and what to bring.

Read the block to someone who did not write it. Ask them to say the outcome and the fence in their own words. If they can, the block is ready. If they recite "partnership," it is not.

The services page names the work. It does not prove who will do it. That is the next page a careful buyer opens, and it should be written as proof of people, not as a memoir. Read [how this company should write its about page](/blog/how-a-b2b-saas-company-should-write-an-about-page) when the offers are clear and the names are still missing.

When you want a second pair of eyes on a page that has to sell a specific offer without swelling into a capability grid, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the blocks you have. The useful part of the call is the fence.
